analytic.title: Real-Time Communication Analysis for Networks with Two-Stage Arbitration

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Current on-chip and macro networks use multi-stage arbitration schemes which independently assign different resources such as crossbar inputs and outputs to individual traffic streams. To use these networks in real-time systems, their worst-case behavior must be proved analytically in order to ensure the required timing guar antees. Current analysis approaches, however, do not capture the multi-stage arbitration accurately. In this paper, we propose an analysis that maps the multi-stage arbitration to a schedulability analysis of multiprocessors with shared resources. This allows the exploitation of knowledge about the worst-case behavior of the individual traffic streams, which is required to provide non symmetric guarantees. Using this scheduling analysis approach, a detailed analysis solution for a common multi-stage arbitration scheme (iSLIP) is presented. Finally, we evaluate the proposed ap proach experimentally and compare it to previous work.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Networks-on-Chip (NoC) are widely recognized as the inter connection paradigm of future mUlti-processor systems on chip (MPSoC) and many-core architectures. The NoC replaces the tra ditional point-to-point and bus connections by a packet-switched fabric of interconnected routers, which are shared among all con nected communication partners as illustrated in Figure la. To com municate with each other, IP blocks send streams of packets that are forwarded from router to router along a specified route. For common architectures, a router receives packets via its inputs and buffers them in FIFO queues. There can be multiple separate FIFO queues or virtual channels (YC) per input module that buffer pack ets from independent streams to avoid head-of-line blocking (Fig-ure 1 b shows 3 FIFOs per input). After computing the destination output port, packets are transmitted via a central switch to the de sired output and then passed to the next router's corresponding in put module. This switch is usually implemented as a crossbar with one port for each input and output module. This implies that the multiple YC buffers at each input share the crossbar and can not be switched simultaneously. In most NoC routers, there is no buffer ing at the output port, which we assume for the remainder of the paper. To reduce buffer sizes, most NoCs (and many macro net works) use wormhole flow-control, where each packet is divided into fix-sized flits and buffer space and arbitration are managed at flit granularity.

In embedded real-time systems, the NoC serves a variety of traffic classes with different requirements, such as guarantees on the maximum communication latency and throughput of individ ual traffic streams in order to meet end-to-end application timing. This is also true for distributed real-time systems employing (e.g. Ethernet-based) macro networks. Note that although macro and on chip networks differ in many details (as a result of differing area, space and energy constraints), they can be considered equivalent in the scope of this paper as two-stage arbitration schemes are used for both. An accurate analysis of the properties of such networks has been identified as an outstanding research problem in NoC design [18]. We address a worst-case analysis of the network for real-time guarantees, as opposed to average-case analysis like [5,11,23]. Guarantees can be derived from the network architecture and uti lization using formal analysis methods which compute the worst possible interference between competing traffic streams and derive upper and lower bounds for latency and throughput.

Interference happens whenever two streams concurrently require the same resource to make progress. For an input-buffered router, three possibilities for interference exist, which are marked in Figure Ib by ellipses. Streams 1 and 2 share the same input module and hence potentially the same buffers (virtual channels), which store blocked traffic. They also enter the central switch which connects input to output ports through the same port. Streams 2 and 3 share the same output port (and inter-router link), which connects adja cent routers. Arbitration mechanisms are used to resolve the above interference. While interference at the input module is independent from the other two resources, the crossbar switch and router output must be allocated together due to the lack of buffers at the output (input-buffered router).

A switch/output arbiter receives requests from individual traffic streams waiting at the input virtual channels for being transmitted to a specified output. The arbiter picks which streams can send by generating a conflict-free mapping, e.g. following a round-robin scheme. This can be done in a central arbiter module which per- forms the arbitration for all requesting streams at once. A central arbiter is equivalent to a scheduler in a real-time computing sys tem, for which the real-time behavior is well understood. The ar bitration is done at flit granularity, so it must be done every flit time (usually I clock cycle in Noes). A central arbiter is slow and area consuming when implemented in hardware, as it must re solve all dependencies concurrently. Alternatively, a non-blocking full crossbar switch can be used, which eliminates interference at the switch input by providing a dedicated input for every virtual channel buffer of every input. This, however, also implies high hardware costs and results in slower switching speeds. Thus, more efficient arbiters such as iSLIP [20] or wave-front-arbitration [30] are used, which split up the arbitration process in multiple (hier archical) steps. Such arbitration schemes can not be treated and analyzed like processor schedulers anymore.

To the best of our knowledge, tight worst-case timing anal ysis methods for such arbitration schemes have not been pro posed. Hence, we present a real-time communication analysis approach for wormhole-switched networks-on-chip (and macro networks) with multi-stage arbitration. It is inspired by the re sponse time analysis of multicore processors with shared resources [27]. Specifically, our approach considers individual traffic injec tion patterns by modeling transmission as flit arrival events. These are characterized by arbitrary worst-case arrival functions which describe the maximum (and minimum) number of flits that can ar rive within a given time interval Ilt. This can be exploited in the analysis to provide non-symmetric guarantees, i.e. to offer certain streams more than their fair share if other streams are known to use 244 less. The proposed analysis accurately considers blocking at the crossbar with arbitration following the iSLIP scheme. Although we limit our analysis to the iSLIP algorithm in this paper, the approach can also be applied to other multi-stage arbitration schemes.

In this paper, we assume that virtual channel buffers are statically allocated to individual traffic streams for streams which require guarantees. This assumption is necessary in networks with worm hole switching where single packets can be distributed over multi ple routers, creating complex head-of-line blocking scenarios dur ing virtual-channel arbitration which lead to very pessimistic guar antees. As a consequence the number of overlapping guaranteed service streams is limited to the number of available virtual chan nels, which is realistic for systems with a limited number of high bandwidth streams. Furthermore, we do not consider a back pres sure flow control for real-time streams in the scope of this paper, i.e. streams whose maximum backlog exceed the local buffer size are deemed infeasible during the analysis. This is an overestima tion, as a back-pressure flow control could handle short-term buffer overloads and hence make the scenario schedulable in some cases (if the previous router can handle the additional delay). Extending the analysis to cover back pressure is left for future work.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: First, we will review related work in Section 2. In Section 3, we will detail the iSLIP arbitration scheme. Section 4 introduces the multicore pro cessor analysis approach and explains the relation to the iSLIP ar bitration scheme. Our proposed analysis is described in Section 5. Finally, we demonstrate our approach in Section 6 and compare it to related work and simulation measurements before we conclude in Section 7.

div.head: RELATED WORK
div.p: Network architectures with support for real-time traffic (Quality of-Service, QoS) reduce or eliminate some (or even all) inter stream interference. This simplifies the analysis and makes the guarantees more accurate, i.e. reduces the overestimation of the worst-case bounds. In practice, QoS is usually achieved by pre allocation of resources and specialized arbitration schemes, which work using time-division multiple-access (e.g. [2 1,7,34]) or pri orities (e.g. [1,2,6,19,15,4]). Such schemes, however, of ten limit the performance of non-real-time applications and im ply an additional hardware overhead. Therefore, this paper focuses on the analysis of router architectures without special support for real-time traffic. Significant research has been done on this topic both for macro-networks and networks-on-chip. [16] presents a worst-case analysis model for wormhole switches to compute max imum latency and minimum guaranteed bandwidth for individual streams. A recursive approach is used which derives latencies at one switch from those at the next (and so forth). This work is ex tended towards networks-on-chip in [25]. Both approaches assume round-robin switch arbitration and first-come-first-serve buffer ar bitration, and hence do not require any hardware QoS support. [8] provides worst-case delay bounds for different arbitration policies (first-come-first-serve and iSLIP). In [12] and [29], analysis ap proaches for the upper delay bound in a network (on-chip) with wormhole switching are presented. These, however, assume a static-priority preemptive scheduling in the routers and hence re quire special routers.
The existing approaches have at least one of the following limi tations, which we overcome by the analysis presented in this paper:

1. The approach assumes a non-blocking full crossbar switch within each router (e.g. [16,12,29,25]). This reduces the potential interference of traffic streams, and no switch con-tention must be considered, but is expensive and slow when implemented in a NoC. Note that the results obtained from an analysis for non-blocking full crossbars are not conservative for crossbars with reduced connectivity! 2. The approach assumes worst-case traffic injection on every stream (e.g. [8]). In other words, it does not exploit poten tially known traffic behavior of individual streams that re duce the worst-case interference. Such approaches can only give symmetric guarantees, i.e. all streams receive the same guarantee (unless additional QoS support is provided).

3. The approach requires the traffic to conform to specific stan dard traffic models, such as being only released periodically with jitter (e.g. [29]). This introduces overestimation in traf fic modeling, which can be avoided by the use of arbitrary traffic models that characterize traffic by worst-case arrival curves (see Sec. 4).

div.head: ISLIP SCHEDULING
div.p: The iSLIP scheduling algorithm was presented in [20] for macro networks. It has since been adapted for use in networks-on-chip, see e.g. [9,13]. The algorithm matches requests of packets to be transferred from input virtual channels to output ports. As an ex ample, consider Fig. lb, where there are three requests: Input 1 -+ Output 2, Input 1 -+ Output 3, and Input 2 -+ Output 3. The match ing is constrained by the limitations of the crossbar switch in that at most one VC per input or output port can be admitted in any cycle. Hence, the first and the second request can not be granted simul taneously. The arbitration is performed by independent arbiters: For every output, a separate arbiter receives requests from the in put modules. Each of those arbiters can only decide which input module it grants to, not which virtual channel. Hence, both arbiters at outputs 2 and 3 could select input 1. Grants from the output ar biter are then arbitrated among the virtual channels within the input modules (since only one flit can leave the input module at a time). Both input and output arbiters follow a fixed round-robin sched ule. Requests are evaluated in a fixed cyclic order, starting from the request that follows the one that was most recently granted. This can be implemented very efficiently in hardware using only a few gates per request and a priority pointer register to the highest pri ority request (see [3]). Note that a fixed round-robin arbiter does not store a history of grants (like a least-recently-served arbiter), so the least recently served request does not necessarily have the highest priority. Hence, we can assume the following property for the arbitration within the iSLIP algorithm: ASSUMPTION 1. A request which is arbitrated by a fixed round-robin arbiter may be blocked at most once by every other concurrent request.
The priority at the output module arbiter is only updated if the cor responding request was also granted at its corresponding input.
The iSLIP algorithm can be described in three steps:
• Step 1 -Request: Each input module sends requests to the arbiters at the outputs to which it has flits.

• Step 2 -Grant: Each output module grants one input mod ule based on a fixed round-robin schedule, giving the low est priority to the most-recently served input. The priority pointer is not updated until the granted input has been ac cepted in the next step.

• Step 3 -Accept: Each input module that received one or more grants selects one grant (and hence output module) 245 based on fixed round-robin schedule. It notifies the granting output module to update its priority pointer. The round-robin pointers in input modules are also updated.

In [20], an iterative algorithm is presented where steps 2 and 3 are repeated multiple times to increase the number of matches. We assume the non-iterative variant of this algorithm (SLIP) in this pa per, because we can not easily make safe assumptions on the subse quent iterations which could be exploited in a worst-case analysis. This is justified as usually only a single iteration can be performed in a NoC environment where low arbitration latencies are crucial. Note that SLIP is starvation free for virtual output queued switches where every input module has exactly one virtual channel per out put port. For input queued switches in general, where two input queues may request the same output, one may starve the other as we will discuss in Sec. 5. [8] includes an analysis of SLIP for vir tual output queued switches. However, it does not exploit known worst-case traffic patterns for individual streams. We will compare [8] to our approach in Sec. 6 We define a stream as a traffic entity which is transported over a network from a given source to a given sink over one or more routers. Furthermore, to distinguish the different types of blocking a stream observes, we define the following sets: DEFINITION 1. Let OutU) be the set of all streams that share the same output port but not the input port with stream i on the router under investigation.

DEFINITION 2. Let In(i) be the set of all streams that share the same input port but not the output port with stream i on the router under investigation. DEFINITION 3. Let Overlap(i) be the set of all streams that share both the same output and input port with stream i on the router under investigation.

Note that the sets Out(i), In(i), and Overlap(i) are mutally dis joint. For a specific stream, we identify the following four sources of blocking in the SLIP algorithm: DEFINITION 4. Let the Direct Output Blocking Time Bfa be the amount of time that stream i is blocked by streams j from other inputs that use the same output (j E Out (i)).

Direct output blocking is resolved in a round-robin fashion. Hence, for each flit, a stream can be blocked at most once by every other input port. In the example, streams 2 and 3 may exhibit mutual direct output blocking. DEFINITION 5. Let the Direct Input Blocking Time BfI be the amount of time that stream i is blocked by streams j destined to other outputs that use the same input (j E In(i)).

In the example, streams 1 and 2 may exhibit mutual direct input blocking if both output 2 and 3 select input 1. DEFINITION 6. Let the Indirect Output Blocking Time BiO be the amount of time that stream i is blocked by streams kfrom other inputs that do not share an input or output with i but directly block streams j sharing i's output (j E Out (i)) at their respective input (k E In(j)).

Since the round-robin priority pointer at the output is not updated as long as a stream is blocked at the input, another stream sharing the same output is also delayed. In the example, stream 3 may ex hibit indirect output blocking from stream 1 via stream 2 (not vice versa!). This would happen if output 3 grants to input 1 (stream 2), but input 1 selects stream 1. Then, stream 3 would not be able to advance, although the resources it requires are unused. DEFINITION 7. Let the Indirect Input Blocking Time Bf! be the amount of time that stream i is blocked by streams j sharing both input and output with stream i (j E Overlap(i)).

Indirect input blocking does not occur in the example, as no streams share both input and output (Overlap(i) = 0). Assume there was another stream 2a parallel to stream 2. Now, when the output grants to the corresponding input, assume the arbiter at the input prioritizes stream 2 first, after which stream 2 receives the lowest priority. Since round-robin schedules in the individual mod ules are not synchronized, output 3 may select input 2 in the next cycle and hence stream 1 is selected at input 1 as stream 2 did not receive its output grant and hence does not request for input arbi tration. This updates the priority pointer in input I, which could lead to stream 2a being "skipped" in having a higher priority than stream 2. Note that the fixed round-robin arbiter only remembers the most-recently served request and grants all other requests fol lowing an internal static priority order. Thus, after stream I has won the arbitration at input I, stream 2 is no longer the most recently served and hence no longer has the lowest priority. The next time output 3 selects input 1, stream 2 may be selected before stream 2a again. Since we make no assumptions on the internal order of the round-robin schedule, we must assume that two "over lapping" streams may always block each other at the input. Hence, indirect input blocking may lead to starvation. This blocking type naturally does not occur for switches with virtual output queuing, which map exactly one VC per input to each output (no overlapping streams).
In the following discussions, we will first consider only the first three types of blocking. The indirect input blocking needs special treatment, which will be discussed separately afterwards.

div.head: ANALOGY OF SCHEDULING MULTIPROCESSOR
div.p: In this section, we will show how the arbitration of multiple de pendent resources can be mapped to the problem of scheduling tasks on multiprocessors with shared resources. For such systems, timing analysis methodologies have recently been investigated [22,27]. First of all, we can interpret the transfer of a flit through the output port of a router as the execution of a task on a processing resource. Hence, every output port of a router corresponds to a processing resource in a multiprocessor system. For every stream that passes through an output port a task is added to this processing resource with a task execution time of one flit transfer time. As suming that a stream passes a router only once, there is exactly one task per router for every stream. Hence, the terms stream and router can be used interchangeably in most situations.

The arrival of a flit at the router then corresponds to a task acti vation at the processing resource, which can be formally described via event models (e.g. periodic with jitter). As the transfer of a flit does not only require the output port, but also exclusive access to the corresponding input port of the crossbar switch, we add a mu tually exclusive shared resource for every input port of a router. In a mUltiprocessor, such a resource would correspond to e.g. a mu tex variable or a shared memory controller. The arbitration scheme used at the output port corresponds to a scheduling policy at the computational resource, while the input arbitration corresponds to a shared resource locking protocol.

Consider the introductory example in Fig. 1 as an illustration. Fig. 2 shows the corresponding multiprocessor system with shared resources following the conventions in [27]. Output ports are shown as gray boxes (processing resources), while input ports are represented by gray hexagons (shared resource). 0,0, and 0, tasks TJ2, TI3, and T23 are added to the correspond ing processing resources (solid circles). Thin arrows represent the mapping to the shared resources. Every task has associated input and output event models lJin/out describing the worst-case activa tion and completion behavior [10]. Tasks TI3 and T23 are mapped to the same resource Out 3 as both corresponding streams share output 3. Similarly, tasks TJ2 and TI3 both use the share resource In 1. In the example, only 3 streams are present, but the figure shows other possible tasks as dashed circles. Note that tasks TIl, Tn, and T33 would imply streams that go back to the port at which they arrived, which does not happen in most routing algorithms. 1 summarizes how the router architecture with multi-stage arbitration maps to the system model of a multiprocessor with shared resources. For the scope of this paper, we will focus on the SLIP arbitration mechanism which arbitrates for two depen dent resources (crossbar input and output ports) in two arbitration stages. Additional arbitration stages would be equivalent to multi ple shared resources being used by each task.

With this analogy, we can map a router with SLIP arbitration to a scheduling analysis model with shared resources. This allows us to use compositional performance analysis to compute the real-time properties of such a system. For single-processor systems, several analysis approaches exist, e.g. Real-Time and Network Calculus [ 3 1, 14] or SymTNS [10] (also called compositional performance analysis). Note that these approaches have already been success fully used to analyze communication such as CAN networks, and [29] even applied the approach to NoCs. However, existing net-work analysis approaches have not included interference on depen dent resources which are present in multi-stage arbitration scheme. [22] has extended the SymTNS approach by providing a solution to include blocking at shared resources. This approach covers a multi processor system with Static Priority Preemptive (SPP) scheduling and Multiprocessor Priority Ceiling Protocol (MCPC) for lock arbi tration. Hence, it must be adapted to match the arbitration strategy of the SLIP algorithm, which has the following properties:
1. Streams (tasks) mapped on an output port (processing re source) are scheduled according to a fixed round-robin schedule.
2. Streams access their input port (shared resource) once at the beginning of their flit-transfer (execution) and for the dura tion of their transfer.
3. Streams which are blocked for their input port do not allow other streams to use the output port (non-preemptive busy waiting).
4. The input port is used in a round-robin fashion, i.e. each stream is blocked at most once by all other streams before it may access the input port after a request.

Although the overall structure of the SLIP algorithm matches mUltiprocessor scheduling, no existing multiprocessor scheduling and arbitration policy covers the above properties. Hence, a cor responding analysis formalism does not exists and must be devel oped, which we will do in the following section. Before doing so, we will recapitulate the system model used for the composi tional performance analysis (SymTNS, [10]), but using the net work terminology (see Ta ble 1). Systems comprise a set streams each assigned to a series of router output ports. At every router, the streams are assumed to be activated by events and for every ac tivation, a stream i is assumed to utilize the router output port for a time delimited by the best-and worst-case transfer times [Ci;C;j.

For the remainder of the paper, we assume for simplicity that all flits have the same transfer time, (Vi, Ci = C; = C), which reflects the common case in real-world (on-chip) networks. The events are characterized by event models which consist of so-called arrival functions, 11t (.M) and 11 ; -(M), describing the maximum and mini mum number of events that can arrive in any given time interval M at a stream i. They fully capture the worst-(and best-)case behavior of streams, such as periodic reactivation, bursts etc. These func tions have pseudo-inverse counterparts, the minimum and maxi mum time intervals 0 ; -(n) and 0 ; + (n) containing n events of stream i. Hence 0-(n) is equal to the smallest Ilt for which 11+ (Ilt) 2: n. Although either 11 or 0 functions are sufficient to express event models, the use of both simplifies certain formulas. Event models are derived from external sources (such as a timer) for the begin ning of a stream or from the analysis of the preceding router for the remaining routers.

To analyze a single router abstracted by the above system model, a critical instant scenario can be constructed for every process ing resource to compute worst-case task behavior and output event models. The computation is based on the concept of a busy window [17,32], which describes the worst-case duration required to pro cess a specific number of activations, including all possible sources of blocking. div.p: Now that we have mapped the SLIP arbitration algorithm to a scheduling problem, we need to derive the corresponding worst case busy window function w;(q) to perform a real-time analysis.

In this section, we will first derive the worst-case busy window for a single router, before we define derived metrics such as worst-case service or latency and discuss the analysis of a complete network. The worst-case busy window will capture the four sources of block ing in SLIP.

div.head: Considering Overlapping Streams
div.p: So far, we have not considered indirect input blocking. This oc curs when two or more streams share both an input and an out put port ("overlapping" streams). At the output arbitration, these streams are indistinguishable as they come from the same input. When this input is granted at the output stage (step 2 of SLIP), the input module decides which stream to serve on a round-robin basis. Since output and input schedules are not synchronized, overlapping streams can potentially "steal" any output grant from each other. If an output grant gets stolen, the priority pointers at the input and out put arbiters are updated. The just served input will become the low est priority on the output arbiter. However, this priority pointer may be changed again by grants from other outputs (for streams that are not overlapping) before the overlapping streams receive their next output grant. Hence, we can not assume that the next output grant will not be stolen again by the same stream. Without further as sumptions on the internal sequence of the fixed round-robin arbiter, the priority of the stream that got stolen from is thus unknown and must conservatively be assumed to be the lowest. Because of this, indirect input blocking can not simply be computed as an additive term to Wi (q) in Equation 2. Instead, we assume that every acti vation on any overlapping stream arriving in the busy window of stream i must be served before stream i is served. Hence, the busy window of stream i extends for every overlapping activation, and at the same time, the amount of overlapping activation depends on the busy window. This mutual dependence can be resolved iteratively, similarly to [27]. THEOREM 2. div.head: Latency
div.p: In a network of routers, the time required from source to sink can be computed. DEFINITION 13. Let maximum end-to-end latency l;(s) be the maximum time required to transfer a single packet with the length of s flits of stream p, from the injection of the first flit at the source to the reception of the last flit at the sink, assuming the packet is injected at maximum rate at the source. PROOF. Assuming a maximum source injection rate, s events are generated at the source within 8 Fi rs t ( p ) (s). The last flit of the packet will then observe at most the worst-case response time at every hop (see Definition II). Since the routing delay is constant with respect to the analysis, it can be simply added as a separate term. 0 Note that Eq. 18 can be an overestimation for bursty event streams, as the last event will most likely not observe the worst case response time at every hop as it is delayed by previous events of the stream. With our analysis being performed at flit level, every packet generates a burst of flits, so the solution proposed in [26] would be a useful extension to our approach.

div.head: Buffer requirements
div.p: For the analysis, we have assumed that the downstream buffers are always large enough to accept new flits from a stream. In other words, a stream can only be blocked at a router due to local inter ference and not due to back pressure from full downstream buffers resulting from downstream interference. The analysis is hence only accurate if the maximum backlog bi (see Eq. 15) does not exceed the available VC buffer capacity. This can be validated during anal ysis.

div.head: EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION
div.p: For evaluation and comparison, we use a Python implementa tion of the proposed SymTNS-based compositional performance analysis ("CPA") and a symmetric analysis that does not exploit in dividual arrival functions ("symmetric"). The symmetric approach follows from our approach for infinite event arrival functions and is equivalent to the solution presented in [8]. However, it extends [8] to allow overlapping streams for switches without virtual output queuing and computing of worst-case response-times and other de rived metrics. For the evaluation, we will focus on a relatively sim ple system from the introductory example (Fig. I and Fig. 2), which is compact enough to be comprehensively displayed but shows all relevant effects of the analysis. For larger systems, the observed results remain valid, and the benefit of the proposed analysis even grows with increasing numbers of interfering streams.

div.head: Single Router
div.p: First, we will evaluate a single router scenario as shown in 3). Fig. 3 shows the single-flit worst-case response times of the four tasks obtained from the analysis using both approaches for increas ing burstiness of task T!3. The results using the approach presented here are shown with up-pointing triangles (.0,), while the results using [8] have down-pointing triangles (\7). At first glance, it can already be seen that our approach improves the worst-case response time for tasks Tl3, Tl3a and T23. For task Tl2, no improvement can be observed, the worst-case response time remains at 5 cycles. The reason is that Tl2 has a low burstiness, so the worst-case always happens at the critical instance where all tasks interfere with each other. In this case, our approach can not exploit any knowledge about the event models of other streams. For T23, a significant re duction of the worst-case response time can be observed for low burstiness of Tl3. With increasing burstiness of Tl3, the blocking inflicted on T23 comes close to that assumed by the symmetric ap proach. For tasks Tl3 and Tl3a, the benefit of our approach in creases with increasing burstiness. This is because the response time linearly increases for the symmetric approach as it can not ex ploit "gaps" left from the other streams that can be used to process a burst faster.

div.head: Complete Network
div.p: To evaluate the analysis on a complete network, we again use the system from the introductory example (Fig. 1 b). For the source activation event models of the individual streams, we use the same models that were used at the router in the previous example, but we fix B to 5. We assume an 5-cycle overhead each for packet gener ation and reception and a 4-cycle overhead per switch for packet routing (see Definition 14). Fig. 4 shows the resulting worst-case end-to-end latencies 1+ (s ) for different packet sizes s using both analysis approaches. Our approach shows no or only slight improvements for the latencies of streams 1 and 3 due to the streams' relatively low burstiness. For streams 2 and 2a, however, a significant reduction of the computed worst-case end-to-end latency can be observed. For validation of our approach, we have implemented a canoni cal router (see [3]) with SLIP scheduling as a cycle-accurate Sys temC model. The modeled router has a flit-time of one cycle and a per-packet delay of 4 cycles, while packet generation and reception require 5 cycles each. We model the introductory example (without stream 2a) using periodic packet injections with the same param eters as in the examples above. Fig. 5 shows a histogram of the latencies of the individual streams measured during the simulation. Vertical lines indicate the computed worst-case latencies of 33, 42 and 41 cycles respectively. The computed worst-case latencies are only 32%, 11 % and 25% (for the respective stream) above the ob served maximum which is very tight for a formal guarantee of a non-trivial network.

div.head: CONCL USION
div.p: In this paper, we have proposed an analysis methodology for net works with multi-stage arbitration mechanisms. We have presented a detailed analysis of the SLIP arbitration algorithm using this ap proach. Compared to existing work, the proposed approach allows the exploitation of known per-stream traffic bounds. This allows the computation of asymmetric guarantees and tighter worst-case response times and transfer latencies. We have evaluated these effects experimentally and validated the analysis results against a cycle-accurate simulation, which showed that the analysis results are conservative with an overestimation of less than 32%.
